body: In 1879, a Paris congress **endorsed** a **sea-level** **canal** across Panama. Godin de Lépinay instead proposed **dams** and **locks**, but his plan was **sidelined**. The French effort foundered **amid** disease and **bankruptcy**. In 1906, John Stevens helped a lock plan prevail 36–31 in the Senate. That decision **conferred** **legitimacy**, not invention. The **decisive** move instead turned **elevation** from an obstacle into a **resource**. Gatun Dam **impounded** the Chagres, creating a lake 26 metres above sea level. Water **submerged** **valleys** and carried ships across much of the **isthmus**; Culebra Cut pierced the remaining **ridge**. Engineers turned a **flood** **hazard** into both reservoir and elevated channel. Each lock's **mitre** **gates** enclosed a vessel. **Operators** opened upper valves; lake water flowed through 18-foot **culverts**, then rose through 100 floor **openings**, limiting **turbulence**. When the chamber reached the next water level, the gate opened. No pump lifted the ship: **gravity** moved water **downhill** while **buoyancy** kept the hull **afloat**. Scale made that cycle **formidable**. Three Gatun steps, one at Pedro Miguel and two at Miraflores **comprised** six **chamber** pairs in **adjacent** **lanes**; each chamber was 110 by 1,000 feet. Lock design fell **chiefly** to Hodges, Schildhauer and Goldmark, while 56,307 people, most from the West Indies, joined the canal's **multinational** **workforce**. Ancon **inaugurated** the **waterway** on 15 August 1914. The **hydraulic** **staircase** carried a price. A traditional transit released about 52 million **gallons** of lake **freshwater** to the ocean. **Concrete** fixed the geometry, but **rainfall** **replenished** the working fluid that every lockage sent through culverts toward the ocean. The **shortcut** was therefore **hydrological**, dependent on Panama's **watershed**: ships climbed the divide on stored rainwater.
